items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: Keith Jarrett and Gary Peacock’s Standards Trio

ctx.x: Not really, because actually it was actually freeing because Manfred Eicher, the producer there, wanted to bring out the best situation, an artistic situation, in music. And it was actually my cymbal work got amplified on a lot of recordings of ECM because Manfred liked detail. And he also liked spontaneity as well as written compositions. And also ECM had a sound that people really liked, and an artistic thing with the covers and it’s still going on today. So it was more about the art of the music rather than…

and they also supported the musicians on their recordings, their touring. So yeah I mean I had a lot of fun recording for ECM. I had my old bands, other good musicians, Keith Jarrett and Gary Peacock’s Standards Trio. So yeah, there was a lot of room to experiment but at a high level of creativity.

Do you save — let me rephrase, I’m sort of surrounded here by a number of your LPs and CDs and I’m wondering if you have a personal collection of Jack DeJohnette recordings? Do you save everything that you do?

items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So Keith joined the band and he was playing Farfisa organ when Chick was in the group.

ctx.x: Right, I saw them as a quartet.

Then Michael Henderson came into the band because Miles really wanted to go into more of an electric funk direction. So Keith joined the band and he was playing Farfisa organ when Chick was in the group. We have documentation of that in the Isle of Wight with that band, which is a great forty-five minutes of music. I’m glad that was done and documented. After that Michael Henderson joined the band and then Miles then started to do… I think that led us up to “Live Evil” which was recorded in Georgetown,…

That’s one of my favorite recordings of the electric period of Miles, Live Evil, because the band is just going all out. It’s like… there’s a term, “grunge” music. Because Keith, the way he played the Fender Rhodes and the Farfisa was just awesome. There was this funky sound, grungy sound, dirty kind of sound. Like Larry Young’s organ with Lifetime. It was a very good blend of improvisation based over grooves that changed all the time, except the “What I Say” which I liked because it was the only time Miles…
